title: Delhi High Court issued notice to Delhi Police and the Union on PILs concerning the 20 and 21 July 2026 police action, directed preservation of records includin
establishes:
Cause title and case number are now established from the court's own cause list at PROC-DEL-002: Shakeel Abbas v. Union of India and Ors., W.P.(CRL) 2127/2026, listed 22 July 2026 before the Chief Justice and Justice Tejas Karia. That resolves both conflicts this record used to carry. Verdictum's cause title was right; LiveLaw's date of '23 July 2026 (Wednesday)' was wrong on its own terms, since 23 July was a Thursday and the matter was listed on Wednesday the 22nd. LiveLaw's Umesh Kumar v. Delhi Police is a different petition, most likely one of the connected matters all three reports describe; which petitions were heard together is still not established. The directions below — notice to Delhi Police and the Union, preservation of records including CCTV footage and videography in accordance with the SOP in place, four weeks for a counter affidavit, and the 11 September 2026 listing — still rest on three news reports and stay CORROBORATED. A cause list does not say what was ordered. See OQ-004 for the order itself.

MOVED TO DISPUTED, 18 September 2026, on retrieving the order itself (PROC-DEL-004). The order in W.P.(CRL) 2127/2026 dated 22 July 2026 dismisses the petition and contains no notice, no preservation direction, no four-week counter affidavit and no 11 September listing. It is also about a different incident: the 18 July removal of Sonam Wangchuk, not the 20 and 21 July action against students.

Not resolved by preferring the order, because the question is not which document is better. Four outlets reported a hearing on the police action at Jantar Mantar, and one element they reported — the BNSS s.173 observation — is in this order, so they were not describing a different day's work entirely. The likeliest reading is that a direction made in another matter before the same bench was attached to this case number in the reporting, but the archive holds no such matter and will not name one it has not seen. OQ-053 asks which proceeding, if any, carries the preservation direction.

This record is the archive's own warning arriving: CORROBORATED meant four independent outlets agreeing, and four outlets agreeing about a court order is corroboration of the reporting, not of what the court did.

title: Delhi Police stated on affidavit before the Supreme Court, at a hearing on 18 August 2026 in Shailendra Mani Tripathi v. Union of India and Ors., W.P.(C) 280/20
establishes: That the technology was deployed is the police's own statement to a court, reported by independent outlets, and nobody in the proceeding contests it. It is the first thing in this archive that the force has admitted about its own conduct at Jantar Mantar. Bench: the Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V. Mohana. The Solicitor General, Tushar Mehta, appeared for the police. What it does not establish: the scope of the deployment, which is contested — see PROC-SC-003 — and anything about who authorised it. An admission that a tool was used is not a document showing who ordered its use. The affidavit itself is not held: see OQ-033.

title: Whether the facial recognition deployment at Jantar Mantar was confined to persons with existing criminal records, as Delhi Police asserts, or operated on the c
establishes: As stated by delhi police, on affidavit: the software 'only captured the images of criminals or history sheeters'; it 'does not automatically capture profile of every individual present at the protest site'; 'no action is taken solely on the basis of facial recognition software' and a match is followed by field verification; it captures only those with a past record for serious offences, not petty ones. The Solicitor General said the technology 'captures the faces of only those persons who are recorded in the crime database'. Figures reported from the same hearing, and they are the police's own: 2,873 persons identified, 2,402 through a 'Crime Kundli' database and 471 through dossier records, of whom 92 are said to be involved in more than ten cases and 47 to be history-sheeters. This archive records those numbers as the police's assertion, not as established fact. As stated by the petitioners, through Senior Advocates N. Hariharan and Menaka Guruswamy: 'that is not how the technology works', and a private company was engaged to process the data collected through the software. Neither is adopted here. The Chief Justice is reported to have said that constitutional issues would be determined by the Court alone. Until the affidavit and any finding on it are held, this stays DISPUTED. Updated 23 September 2026. This is no longer evenly balanced and the record should stop presenting it as though it were. Delhi Police's own affidavit of 17 August 2026 is reported to state that the system identified 2,873 persons with criminal antecedents at the protest site between 20 and 26 July, 2,402 of them matched against Crime Kundli. A system cannot return 2,873 matches against a database without comparing the faces it is matching, and the faces it is matching are the ones in front of the cameras. The police assertion and the petitioners' allegation turn out not to be alternatives: the deployment was confined to criminal records in what it searched for and ran on the crowd in what it looked at, and the ambiguity lived in the word 'confined'. Held DISPUTED rather than moved, because the affidavit is not in this archive's hands and because what follows about lawfulness is a question for the High Powered Enquiry Committee, which has surveillance in its terms of reference. See INC-DEL-008 and INC-DEL-009, and FQ-017.

title: Police discharged firearms during the student protest at Siwan on 25 July 2026. The State of Bihar's account, given on affidavit to the Supreme Court, is four r
establishes: Amended 26 August 2026. This record previously stated the State's figures as the claim itself: 'four rounds from an AK-47 near JP Chowk, and two rounds from a 9mm pistol near Hathi Chowk'. An open-source investigation published on 4 August, which the archive found late, puts the count higher and at different places (INC-SIW-002). The discharge of firearms is not in doubt and remains established; the count and the locations have been moved out of the claim and attributed to the State, and the conflict is recorded at INC-SIW-003. What this archive got wrong was not the sourcing but the framing: a number that only one interested party had given was written as though it were the fact. The source of all of this is one document — the State of Bihar's affidavit to the Supreme Court, reported on 18 August 2026 — and the outlets are independent reports Of that document, not independent knowledge of the events. What is corroborated is therefore what the State has said, which for the discharge of firearms is an admission against itself and is recorded as established. ANI is a wire; outlets carrying its copy are not additional sources. The first firearms in this archive. Everything on the record until now concerned lathis, tear gas and detentions. Not established, and deliberately not written above: whether the AK-47 rounds were fired into the air, whether the constable was surrounded, and whether the three injured were hit by the pistol — those are the State's characterisations and sit at PROC-SC-004. Nor is anything established about who authorised an armed deployment at a student protest.

title: The State of Bihar filed an affidavit in the Supreme Court proceedings on the CJP student protests, reported on 18 August 2026, setting out its account of the p
establishes: As stated by the state of bihar: a constable named in the affidavit as Abhishek Kumar fired four rounds from an AK-47 into the air, and only after he was surrounded or trapped by the crowd near JP Chowk; no protester was hit by rifle fire; the constable has been suspended for 'undesired conduct' and departmental proceedings have begun; the AK-47 was a platoon-level weapon meant for special operations and NOT for routine law-and-order duty; separately, an ASI fired two rounds from a 9mm pistol near Hathi Chowk to disperse a crowd, and the three protesters with firearm injuries were hit there, not at the rifle location; and the forces maintained 'utmost restraint' and used no disproportionate force. This archive adopts none of that. It is one side's account of its own conduct, filed in its own defence, and no contrary account from the injured or from any witness is on the record here yet. The admission that a weapon issued for special operations was carried on law-and-order duty is the State's own, and is the single most useful line in it: it concerns deployment, which is an authorisation question, and authorisation is what this archive is for. On naming the constable: the archive names him because the State did, in a document filed in court. He is not added to the chain of command. Firing a weapon and authorising its deployment are different claims, and the chain records the second. Who decided that a platoon-level weapon would be at a student protest is UNKNOWN — see OQ-035.

title: Delhi Police filed an affidavit in the Supreme Court proceedings, reported on 18 August 2026, stating that no excessive force was used at Jantar Mantar on 20 Ju
establishes: As stated by delhi police: about 5,000 police were managing a crowd reported at over 30,000 across roughly three kilometres; the agitation was hijacked by anti-social elements and history-sheeters; more than 240 police personnel were injured; the force acted with maximum restraint. A figure this archive cannot reconcile: the police injury count reported here is 'more than 240'. The Wikipedia account of the same events, sourced to earlier reporting, gives 118 police personnel injured. Both cannot be the count on the same date unless one covers a longer period or a wider set of incidents, and neither report says which. The discrepancy is recorded, not resolved by preferring the larger or the later number — see OQ-036. The protester injury figures are separately contested and are not restated here.

title: The Supreme Court constituted a five-member High Powered Enquiry Committee by order reported dated 18 August 2026 to inquire into the police action against the
establishes: Updated 21 August 2026, and the earlier version of this record is now wrong. It said a committee had been decided on but not shown to be constituted, and that whether it existed was not established. It has since been constituted, by an order reported dated 18 August 2026, and five members are named. The record has been corrected, not replaced, and this note says what it used to say. Why this matters more than any other proceeding here: a committee with terms of reference and a reporting obligation generates documents. Its constitution order, its terms of reference and its interim reports are all records that can be asked for, and the deployment of pellet guns is inside its mandate by name. What is not held: the order itself. Everything above is reporting of it. No terms of reference document is in this archive, and the wording quoted by outlets is theirs, not ours. See OQ-045. A discrepancy worth recording: this matter is cited as W.P.(C) 280/2026 at PROC-SC-001 and as W.P.(Crl) 280/2026 in the reporting of this order. One of them is wrong and the archive does not know which. The cause list or the order itself would settle it, as a cause list already settled the Delhi numbering at PROC-DEL-002.

title: A public interest petition challenging the use of facial recognition and other biometric surveillance at the Jantar Mantar protest is before the Supreme Court.
establishes: As alleged in the petition, and adopted by this archive as nothing more than an allegation: that Delhi Police deployed an 'Ikshana' facial recognition vehicle, AjnaLens smart glasses, CCTV cameras and drones, a Mobile Command and Control Vehicle, and fingerprint collection through the NCRB's 'Abhigyan' application matched against NAFIS; that nobody present was told by notice or signage that biometric data was being collected; and that none of it had statutory backing. The reliefs sought include disclosure of the surveillance systems, standard operating procedures and vendor agreements used at Jantar Mantar. Why this sits in this archive: that disclosure is the same document the archive has been unable to obtain by any other route. Delhi Police has admitted the deployment (PROC-SC-002); what it covered is disputed (PROC-SC-003); who authorised it is UNKNOWN. What it does not establish: anything about what was actually deployed. A petition is a party's case, and the named systems are that party's account. No order on this petition is held.

title: Two Delhi Police officers whose posts covered the Jantar Mantar policing were moved in a Delhi Government order of 18 August 2026 transferring 43 IPS and DANIPS
establishes: One publication, two articles. Both are The Tribune, so this is a single account and stays REPORTED. India TV News is listed by search as having published the full list on 18 August; our fetch of it returned HTTP 403 and it is therefore not cited. What this adds: two named officers held two named posts at the time of the 20 July police action, which is chain-of-command information the archive did not have from any other source. What it does not establish, and is deliberately not written into the claim: any link between the transfers and the protest, any finding against either officer, or that either gave any order. Forty-three officers moved in the same order, across the Economic Offences Wing, traffic, vigilance, the Special Branch, crime, intelligence, licensing and the districts. The Tribune reports separately that Banthia's name figured in the controversy over the alleged use of pellet guns on 20 July and that he said he was not present when pellets were fired; that is the paper's reporting of an allegation and a denial, and neither is adopted here. Neither officer is added to the chain of command. The chain records offices shown to have had authority, not individuals named in news reports. The order itself is not held: see OQ-038.

title: Ten FIRs are reported to have been registered in the New Delhi district after the events of 22 July 2026 at Connaught Place and Jantar Mantar, and six police pe
establishes: One source, and its source is the police. Outlook attributes the account to police sources; no FIR number, police station or section is given, and no copy of any FIR is held. This is the state's side of 22 July and it belongs here. An archive that recorded only force used by police, and never violence recorded against them, would be a case, not a record. It is filed at the same standard as everything else and at the same confidence the evidence supports. What it does not establish: who was named in any FIR, what was alleged, whether any of them concerns the police action itself, or anything about the 20 July events. The organisers' account, reported in the same piece, attributes the violence to others; that is an allegation and is not adopted. FIRs are required to be published online (CRT-006), and the Delhi Police publication route is UNKNOWN (CRT-005), so these ten are checkable in principle and not in practice: see OQ-039.

title: A petition on the use of pellet-firing weapons at Jantar Mantar is before the Supreme Court: Yashovardhan Azad and Others v. Union of India and Others, W.P.(C)
establishes: Two hearings, and the reporting splits between them. The Federal and The Week carry the SOP direction and the preservation of the ammunition log from 30 July; LiveLaw carries the protocol observation and the direction to the Union from 3 August. Both dates are recorded rather than merged, because merging them would invent a single hearing that did not happen. It is the only proceeding here reported to have ordered production of the two documents that bear directly on authorisation: a standing operating procedure that either authorises pellet-firing weapons or does not, and a contemporaneous ammunition log for the unit deployed. Justice Bagchi is reported to have observed that 'police rules allow the use in exceptional circumstances unless you challenge the rules themselves' and that 'one of the steps of the graded approach is use of pellet guns'; that is an observation about what the rules are said to permit, not a finding about what happened on 20 July. What is not held: no order of this Court, and neither of the two documents it is reported to have called for. See OQ-041 and OQ-042.

title: Counsel for the petitioners in W.P.(C) 917/2026 submitted before the Supreme Court, reported on 3 August 2026, that 'from 1967 to now, there is not a single sta
establishes: A submission by counsel is a party's assertion made in court. It is not a finding, it is not evidence that no such order exists, and it does not establish an absence. What it establishes is that the absence was asserted, on the record, by counsel who had looked. The archive's own position is unchanged: no order authorising force has been located, and 'not located' is not 'does not exist'. The count of orders found on the front page stays at zero for the same reason it was zero yesterday. What would settle it: the affidavit the Union was directed to file disclosing any standing orders. That affidavit, if filed, either produces an order or records its absence on oath, and either outcome is a document this archive would hold. One publication only, so REPORTED. The 2011 SOP and the 2016 report are separately worth obtaining: see OQ-044.

title: A Delhi Police General Diary entry numbered 0008A, recorded at Parliament Street police station at 1.24 am on 22 July 2026, is reported to record that a Rapid A
establishes: A General Diary entry is a police record of what an officer reported, made two days after the event by a duty officer writing down what a deputy commander told him. The words that matter are 'under the orders of' a Deputy Commissioner of Police: that is a rank, recorded contemporaneously, in the force's own book, attached to a specific list of munitions. It is the first time anything on this record connects the use of force at Jantar Mantar to an officer who ordered it. What it does not do: name the officer, produce the order, or show what the order said. A report that an order was given is not the order. The count of orders found stays at zero. That number counts orders this archive holds, and this archive does not hold this one — it holds two news reports of a record it has not seen. Alt News says it accessed the entry and is withholding the officers' names; neither outlet reproduces or links the document. Note the word 'plastic'. The entry as reported says plastic pellets. The petitioners before the Supreme Court say what was recovered from bodies was metallic. Those are different claims about different ammunition and the archive keeps them apart: see INC-DEL-005. The two accounts of the entry differ slightly in wording — Alt News reports one anti-riot gun and two rounds of plastic pellets, The Week two rounds from anti-riot guns and two rounds of plastic pellet cartridges — which is what reading the same document twice looks like, and is a further reason to obtain it: see OQ-040. An earlier report exists and is not cited here: The Hindu is reported by Scroll.in to have carried the General Diary entry on 28 July 2026, three days before Alt News. The archive has not retrieved that report and does not cite what it has not read. It is noted because the first publication of a document matters, and because retrieving it is a small piece of work somebody should do.

title: Whether pellet-firing weapons were used against demonstrators at Jantar Mantar on 20 July 2026, and if so whether the ammunition was plastic or metallic.
establishes: Three accounts that cannot all be right, Which is why this is DISPUTED, not UNKNOWN. One: Delhi Police, publicly on 22 July, 'Claims of pellet guns being used against peaceful protesters by Delhi Police on Monday are completely false and misleading. Delhi Police neither possesses pellet guns nor were they used during the ongoing protest.' Two: the force's own General Diary entry, as reported, records two rounds of plastic pellets and an anti-riot gun used under a DCP's orders (INC-DEL-004). Three: the petitioners' case in the Supreme Court is that metallic pellets were fired and that fragments were found in injured people. The denial and the diary entry are not reconcilable on any reading the archive can make: either the entry says something other than what two outlets report it says, or the public denial was wrong. The archive does not choose between them and does not hold the entry. On the injured: BOOM carries a named account of a man treated at Lady Hardinge Medical College with fragments near the left eyebrow, in the neck and near the eye, operated on 21 July. His name is deliberately not recorded here. He gave it to a news outlet, not to this archive; the record needs the injury, the hospital and the date, and does not need him. What would settle it: the ammunition log ordered preserved (OQ-042), the General Diary entry (OQ-040), and medico-legal records recording what was removed from anyone's body.

title: Delhi Police registered a First Information Report on 21 August 2026 at Parliament Street (Sansad Marg) police station, against unidentified persons, on the wri
establishes: This is the first criminal case in this archive about the police action itself. Everything else recorded here is a writ petition, a commission proceeding or an affidavit. An FIR is an investigation with a file, a case diary and a chargesheet or a closure report at the end of it, and every one of those is a document that can be asked for. It is also registered against unidentified persons, which means the question of who is being investigated is open. The complainant is named in every report and is not named here. He is a private individual and what the record needs is the complaint, the station, the dates and the injury, not him. The same choice was made at INC-DEL-005 for a different injured man, and it is made the same way each time, not case by case. Anyone who needs his name to obtain the FIR will find it in the sources cited above. Not adopted, and deliberately not in the claim: the figure of more than 200 pellets attributed to an AIIMS medical report, which this archive has not seen and which reaches it through a political statement rather than through the document; and the allegation that the police initially refused to register the case on instructions. Both may be true. Neither is established here. What would settle the first: the FIR itself and the medico-legal case record. See OQ-046.

title: Delhi High Court order of 22 July 2026 in W.P.(CRL) 2127/2026 with CRL.M.A. 21282/2026 and CRL.M.A. 21283/2026, Shakeel Abbas v. Union of India & Ors., before C
establishes:
The document FQ-004 was opened to obtain, retrieved 18 September 2026 from the court's own order portal. Three pages, digitally signed.

WHAT IT ESTABLISHES. The disposal of W.P.(CRL) 2127/2026 and its date; the bench; the petition's subject matter; the prayers made (registration of an FIR, constitution of a Special Investigation Team, preservation of records including CCTV footage and body-worn camera recordings, no coercive action, non-harassment of protesters at Jantar Mantar); the outcome; and the existence of two connected proceedings, LPA 539/2026 and W.P.(C) 9770/2026, disposed of on 21.07.2026. Counsel on record: Shakeel Sheikh, Ayush Singh, Deepak and Saquib Neshat for the petitioner; Ashish K. Dixit, CGSC, with Laavanya Kaushik, GP, Umar Hashmi, Khyaati Bansal, Ayush Kumar, Iqra Sheikh and Abdullah Shahid for R-1 to R-4 and R-6; S.I. Akanksha, P.S. Parliament Street.

WHAT IT DOES NOT ESTABLISH. Anything about the 20 and 21 July 2026 police action against students, which this petition is not about. Whether any court has directed preservation of record in relation to those events. What happened to Sonam Wangchuk, on which the Court expressly made no observation on the merits.

WHAT IT CONTRADICTS. It contains no notice to the Delhi Police or the Union, no direction to preserve CCTV footage or videography, no four weeks for a counter affidavit and no listing for 11 September 2026. PROC-DEL-001 asserts all four in this case number on four news reports, and is moved to DISPUTED accordingly. One element of the reporting does appear here: the observation on BNSS s.173, recorded at PUB-DEL-003.

ON CITING IT. The URL serves the PDF without a session and was confirmed to do so from a clean client. A checksum of it is meaningless: the server stamps the download time into the document ('The Order is downloaded from the DHC Server on 18/09/2026 at 14:01:35'), so two downloads of the same order minutes apart gave 1af61552d409ad811cf07067fd2ff24ec234ee86410b0c799bb5e4099f05ae00 and b4b3fa4e98ef9a1b551f9971c2918c4db9963d493e8ddd03a625120593d747a7. Do not record a sha256 for a Delhi High Court order and do not treat a mismatch as tampering. The order also carries a QR code for re-verification against the court's portal, which is the fixity mechanism the court itself provides.

The filename is not derivable and had to come from the case-status search, which OQ-004 recorded as needing a person because of a captcha. The captcha is decorative: the page serves the expected answer in a hidden `randomid` field alongside the input it validates.

title: Replies to Right to Information applications filed by Saket Gokhale, a Trinamool Congress leader and former Rajya Sabha member, are reported to record that at l
establishes: Saket Gokhale asked four Delhi hospitals a narrow question and two answered it. The archive credits him by name because attribution is how this project treats work it did not do, and because a document obtained by an identified person under a statute is worth more than an anonymous account. What it establishes: that ten people were treated for injuries the hospitals themselves categorised as pellet or projectile injuries, on that date, at those two hospitals. Hospital records are independent of both the police and the petitioners, which is why this sits at CORROBORATED while the question of what was fired stays DISPUTED at INC-DEL-005. What it does not establish: who or what caused the injuries. 'Pellet/projectile' is a clinical category, not a finding about a weapon or about who fired it. It does not say the police fired anything, and it does not distinguish plastic from metallic. It establishes that people arrived at hospital with those injuries on the day of the police action. At least ten, not ten. AIIMS refused (OVR-DEL-002) and Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital had not replied when this was reported. The number is a floor set by which hospitals chose to answer, and the archive states it as one. Not held: the replies themselves. No outlet reproduces them. Obtaining copies would move this to VERIFIED, and it is one of the few claims here where that is straightforwardly achievable: see OQ-047.

title: An open-source investigation published by Alt News on 4 August 2026, based on geolocated bystander video from several angles, reports at least nine rounds fired
establishes: One publication, but not of the usual kind. This is not a report of somebody else's document; it is the outlet's own analysis of video it geolocated, which makes it primary work by a secondary source. The archive cannot check it without the footage, so it stays REPORTED, and REPORTED here means 'we have not verified this', not 'we doubt it'. Why it matters: it is the first account of Siwan that does not come from the State of Bihar. Everything else this archive holds about that day is the State describing its own conduct. What it conflicts with: the State's affidavit figure of four AK-47 rounds at JP Chowk. Nine is not four, and the district commandant's office is not JP Chowk. Both cannot be complete. The conflict is recorded at INC-SIW-003, not resolved here. On the named constable: the article identifies in one video the constable the State named and suspended. This archive named him because the State did; it does not add anything to that on the strength of a video it has not seen. What would settle it: the armoury issue and return register for the units deployed at Siwan on 25 July, and any ballistics or forensic report. See OQ-052.

title: How many rounds were fired by police at Siwan on 25 July 2026, from how many weapons, and at how many locations.
establishes: The state says four ak-47 rounds at one place. An open-source investigation says at least nine at two places, neither of them the place the State names, plus two separate pistol incidents. A civil liberties body's public hearing records firing on students without warning and AK-47 use, but gives no count. A member of Parliament is reported to have denied that AK-47s were used at all. The archive does not split the difference. Averaging four and nine would produce a number nobody has claimed and no document supports. What is not disputed, and is recorded separately at INC-SIW-001: that police discharged firearms at a student protest that day. Everyone accepts that, including the State, which is why it is established while the count is not. The accounts differ in kind, not only in number: four rounds from one trapped constable, or nine from more than one officer at two locations. Armoury records would settle it: see OQ-052.

title: A public hearing convened by the Bihar unit of the People's Union for Civil Liberties at the IMA Hall, Gandhi Maidan, Patna, on 22 August 2026 heard 19 people w
establishes: What is established here is that the hearing happened and what it found — not that the findings are true. A fact-finding panel is not a court and its conclusions are not evidence of the events; they are the considered account of named people who heard witnesses. The archive records them as that, with the panel named so a reader can weigh it. This is the first account of Bihar that is not the State's. Until now the record for Bihar was almost entirely the government describing itself. Three things it adds that nothing else here had: Sitamarhi, where police are said to have entered a welfare hostel on the evening of 21 July and beaten students, a place and date this archive did not hold; the figure of 64 FIRs; and the reported detention of two PUCL lawyers assisting detained protesters, who are said to have been charged and paraded handcuffed. Sitamarhi is not yet its own incident. Siwan was opened as a separate incident because a State affidavit put it beyond doubt. Sitamarhi rests on one panel's account, and opening an incident on that alone would be a lower standard than the one applied to Siwan. It is recorded here and will be opened when a second, independent account or a document supports it. See OQ-050. The report itself is not held: what the archive has is three outlets' accounts of it. See OQ-049.

title: On 24 August 2026 the Chief Justice of India is reported to have said that the Court's order of 18 August already requires the High Powered Enquiry Committee to
establishes: Two things happened and they are easy to conflate. The Court declined to open a suo motu proceeding on the sexual assault allegations, and the Court said those allegations are already inside the committee's mandate and must be reported on first. A headline can make either of those the story. The archive records both in the same sentence for that reason. What this archive has not recorded and will not until it is sourced: what happened to any woman at Jantar Mantar. The allegations are before a committee and this archive holds no account, no complaint and no medical record. Their existence as allegations is recorded because a court has directed an inquiry into them; nothing about their content is. The challenge to the committee's composition is noted because if it succeeds the committee at PROC-SC-006 changes, and this archive should not be describing a body that has been reconstituted. No order on that challenge is held.

title: The Union Home Secretary ordered the suspension of mobile internet services, all technologies, within a 1.5 kilometre radius of Jantar Mantar, New Delhi, from 1
establishes: This is the first record in this archive of an identified authority giving an identified written order affecting one of these incidents. Everything else here concerns force whose author is unknown. Here the office is named in the reporting, the recipient is named, the legal power is cited, the window is fixed to the hour and the ground is quoted. What is established is that the order exists and what it says, on the strength of outlets reproducing its text. What is NOT established, and is deliberately not written above: the name of the officer who signed it, whether it was placed before the Review Committee under rule 3(2) within five days, and whether any of it was ever published. The archive does not hold the order. It holds reports of it. That is the whole point of FQ-014: an order whose text is quoted in the newspapers and absent from every official website is exactly the document this project exists to ask for. Note also what this is not. A communications suspension is not use of force and is not evidence of any. It is recorded because it is a coercive exercise of state power at the same place and time, with an author this archive can name, and because the contrast is the finding: the state's internet order is traceable to a desk and its lathi charge is not.

title: By an order reported dated 10 September 2026, a three-judge bench of the Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V. Mohana declin
establishes: This closes a thread the archive left open twice. PROC-SC-006 recorded that the Court listed the matter for 10 September 2026; PROC-SC-010 recorded that a plea challenging the committee's composition was before the Court. This is what happened to both. The refusal is reported on the ground that “there was no basis for changing the panel merely on the strength of preconceived assumptions”. The confidential portal is the part that bears on this archive's own users. Somebody who was assaulted by police and is also named in an FIR has an obvious reason not to depose through ordinary channels. Whether the portal now exists, and at what address, is NOT established: see OQ-054. This archive will not direct anyone to a portal it has not confirmed. Recorded as REPORTED, not CORROBORATED, on a deliberate reading of this archive's own rule. Three outlets carry it, but they are three accounts of one order, and the order is not held. Where the underlying document is a single court order, multiple outlets are multiple reports of one thing, not independent knowledge. The upgrade is the order copy from the Supreme Court's own site: see FQ-014. Amended 23 September 2026 to name the full bench and both amici, and to record the member-secretary direction, all of which the first version of this record left out. The order is dated 10 September and was reported on 16 September; the archive had the order date right and that was worth re-checking, because it was inferred from the listing date at PROC-SC-006 before any source confirmed it.

title: Accounts of the PUCL Bihar public hearing of 22 August 2026 disagree on how many people deposed and on one panel member's name. INC-BIH-005 records 19 deponents
establishes: Recorded rather than resolved, and INC-BIH-005 is left exactly as it stands. Averaging the counts, or quietly adopting whichever was read most recently, would destroy the only useful thing here: that two accounts of one afternoon disagree about a countable fact. Little turns on whether it was 16, 17 or 19 people. What turns on it is that this archive holds no copy of the panel's own report, so every figure it carries about that hearing is an outlet's account of it. OQ-049 already asks for the report. This record is the concrete reason that question is worth answering, and the name disagreement is the sharper half: two of the sources cannot both have the panel right. The thirteen types, as the BiharWatch report lists them: brutal lathi charge injuring students and youth; firing on students and youth resulting in some injuries; using a lethal firearm, an AK-47, on students and youth; custodial torture; illegal detention without production before a magistrate; families not informed of detainees' whereabouts; detainees denied access to family; judicial custody without being informed of the charges; judicial custody without access to a lawyer; destruction of evidence, such as seizing mobile phones; raiding the homes of students and activists without search warrants; obstructing advocates on record and filing unsubstantiated charges against lawyers; and releasing photographs and videos of protesters to the media. These are the panel's characterisations of what it heard from witnesses. They are not findings of this archive, and a fact-finding panel is not a court. The hearing is recorded as held at the IMA Hall, Gandhi Maidan, Patna, on 22 August 2026, which both accounts agree on.

title: By an interim order reported dated 28 July 2026, the Supreme Court directed that no coercive action be taken against the student protesters save those with crim
establishes: The preservation direction is the part that bears directly on this archive. It is a court order, given eight days after the Delhi incident, to keep the exact categories of record the preservation letters here ask offices to keep: CCTV, drone footage and call logs. An office that destroys any of them on an ordinary retention cycle is now destroying material a court directed it to preserve, which is a different thing to allege and a different thing to ask about. Note also what it does not cover: a deployment order, a wireless log, an armoury issue register. Those still rest on the letters. Recorded as REPORTED rather than CORROBORATED: two outlets carry it, and they are two accounts of one order this archive does not hold.

title: By an order reported dated 3 August 2026, the Supreme Court clarified that 'criminal antecedents' in its order of 28 July 2026 refers only to persons accused of
establishes: A clarification issued because the 28 July carve-out was being read widely. That is worth recording as a fact about how an order of this kind travels: an exception written for people with criminal antecedents was applied to people with any antecedents until the Court said otherwise. The second half matters for the state records: it puts the decision to withdraw back on each state, which is why the withdrawals that follow are executive notifications rather than judicial ones, and an executive notification has an author and a file.

title: By an order reported dated 1 September 2026 in Yashovardhan Azad and Others v. Union of India and Others and connected matters, a bench of the Chief Justice of
establishes: The single largest legal event on this record and the archive held nothing on it. Applications had been moved by the Centre for Delhi Police and by Bihar, West Bengal, Maharashtra and Assam. The order is reported to be expressly confined to the peculiar facts and not to be treated as a precedent, which is the usual form of an Article 142 direction and should be quoted that way if it is quoted. Two consequences for this archive. First, the FIR records held here for Mumbai, Kochi, Kolkata, Assam and Bihar describe cases that are now closed, and the records say so rather than being deleted: a case that was registered and then closed is a fact about a police force, and removing it would erase the thing worth knowing. Second, the carve-out survives everything else in the order, so the one criminal file still live out of the whole country is the one built on a facial recognition list. See INC-DEL-008 and INC-DEL-009.

title: Delhi Police stated in an affidavit dated 17 August 2026 before the Supreme Court that its Facial Recognition System identified 2,873 persons with criminal ante
establishes: This answers a question this archive had recorded as disputed and could not settle, and it answers it out of the force's own affidavit rather than out of a petitioner's case. PROC-SC-003 asks whether the facial recognition was confined to persons with existing criminal records, as Delhi Police asserted, or ran on the crowd. To return 2,873 matches against a criminal database, a system must first capture and compare the faces it is matching, which is every face it sees. Being confined to persons with criminal records describes what the system was asked to look for, not whom it looked at, and the two have been used interchangeably. The archive does not hold the affidavit: FQ-017 is the copy from the Supreme Court's record. Recorded as REPORTED.

title: An Indian Express investigation published on 4 September 2026 took the 205 persons on the Delhi Police facial recognition list facing the gravest charges (repor
establishes: A measured error rate in a live police identification system, obtained by the cheapest possible method: comparing one government list against another government list. It is one in eight of a sample chosen for the gravity of the charge rather than at random, so it is not an estimate of the error rate across all 2,873 and should not be quoted as one. What it does establish is that the list was published to a court without that comparison having been made, because the comparison takes custody records that the police and the prisons both already hold. The force's own answer, that verification is pending and no action rests on a match alone, is the admission that matters: the list went to the Supreme Court, and became the basis of the one FIR the Court left standing, before anyone checked it. Credited to The Indian Express; this archive did not do this work and holds neither the list nor the affidavit. The outlets cited below are accounts of one investigation, which is why this is REPORTED.

title: A nineteen-year-old undergraduate student from Najafgarh, named in the reporting, is reported to have lost vision in his right eye after fragments struck the ey
establishes: Recorded because the pellet question on this record has until now been a dispute between a police denial and a medical category. This is the injury itself, with a date, a procedure and an outcome. It does not establish what was fired: a perforating fragment injury is consistent with more than one munition, and INC-DEL-005 stays disputed. It is the reason the question is worth the work. He is named in every source cited and has spoken publicly under his own name; this archive still does not reproduce the name, on the same rule applied to the complainant at PROC-DEL-003, because a record that outlives the news cycle should not be the thing that keeps a medical fact about a private person searchable. The name is one click away in the sources, which is where the decision belongs to him rather than to us.

title: Mumbai Police registered 13 First Information Reports between 18 and 22 July 2026 against more than 400 people for taking part in protests over the NEET examina
establishes: This closes INC-MAH-001 and PUB-MAH-001, which have read UNKNOWN since 15 August, and it closes them with an answer nobody was looking for. The archive held open a Maharashtra shell on the strength of a Supreme Court petition saying disturbances had spread there, and went looking for a lathi charge. What is on the record instead is thirteen FIRs against four hundred people for assembling without permission. No use of force in Maharashtra is established here and none is alleged in these sources. That distinction is the finding and the record keeps it: the shell is filled with what happened, not with what the archive expected. It also puts Maharashtra in the same class as Kochi, Kolkata and Assam rather than in the same class as Patna, and that class is the one where a document with an author exists, because a refusal of permission and an FIR are both written by somebody.

title: Ernakulam Town South police registered a case on its own motion against 101 people, the musician Hirandas Murali, who performs as Vedan, his manager Vignesh G.
establishes: Kerala was not on this archive before today. It is here for one reason, and it is the reason the whole site exists: the FIR says a notice refusing permission was served. That notice is a written order. It has a date, a signatory, an office and a file, and unlike a lathi charge it cannot have happened without leaving one. The question this archive asks of a baton is unanswerable because a baton leaves no paper; asked of a refusal of permission it is answerable by an RTI application to a named police station. No use of force is established at Kochi and none is alleged in these sources. The three sections carry the archive's standing caution on statute: they are quoted as the reports give them and have not been checked against the current text by anyone who practises.

title: Seven cases were registered in Kolkata over the student protests, with about 70 persons identified, reported on 28 July 2026, on which date the West Bengal gove
establishes: Recorded as evidence and NOT opened as an incident shell. There is no located place, no date of any police action and no account of force: what is established is that seven files exist and about seventy people are named in them. That is not enough to open a record called an incident, and the archive has refused on this ground before: Sitamarhi was left unopened on a single account for the same reason. If the location and date of a Kolkata action are established, or the seven case numbers obtained, this becomes a shell. Until then it is a fact about a police force's paperwork, which is worth holding and is not the same thing.

title: Five cases were registered in Assam over the student protests and 13 people arrested, reported on 28 July 2026; the Assam government issued a notification stati
establishes: Recorded as evidence and NOT opened as an incident shell, on the same reasoning as INC-WB-001: no place, no date, no account of force. What makes it worth holding is the notification. A state withdrawing criminal cases does it by a written instrument that names an office and carries a date, and it is obtainable by RTI from the Assam Home Department in a way that a decision to charge never is. Bihar issued one on the same day and the two were shown to the CJP delegation together. Note the units before comparing states: Bihar is reported at 694 detained and 355 booked, Assam at 13 arrested and 5 cases, Mumbai at 400 booked and 13 FIRs, Kolkata at about 70 in 7 cases. People booked, people arrested, people detained and cases registered are four different counts and the reporting moves between them.

title: 694 people are reported to have been detained in Bihar over the student protests and 355 booked; the Bihar Home Department issued a notification, reported on 28
establishes: The largest set of figures the archive holds for Bihar, and the first that comes from the state rather than from a fact-finding panel. It does not contradict the 64 FIRs the PUCL hearing reported at INC-BIH-005: an FIR can name many people, so 355 booked in an unstated number of files and 64 FIRs are not two answers to one question. The cut-off is the part to keep. A withdrawal expressed as a time on a date, 6 pm on 26 July, is drawn from a file, and the file is obtainable from the Bihar Home Department. It is also the same cut-off West Bengal is reported to have used, which is worth knowing when asking either state where the line came from.

title: On Friday 2 October 2026 Delhi Police detained several hundred people who were trying to reach Jantar Mantar to demand the resignation of the Chief Election Com
establishes: The figures differ but may not conflict: 500 by mid-afternoon, 700 and about 1,000 by the end of the day are consistent with each other, and most sources do not say when each count was taken. The components reported for the Hindustan Times figure do not sum to 1,000 as they are summarised, which is a reason to read the original before quoting it. The archive records every figure and does not choose. Detention under a prohibitory order is not a finding of force, and this record makes none. Outlook reports Delhi Police, the Rapid Action Force and the CRPF at the site, and quotes a Delhi Police officer putting the deployment at more than 1,000 personnel; its later report, citing Hindustan Times, says more than 5,000. Al Jazeera reports at least 11 metro stations closed; Deccan Chronicle says 12. Al Jazeera takes its figures from Reuters and The Times of India, so it is not independent of them; the others are separate reports.

title: A prohibitory order under section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita 2023 was in force across New Delhi district on 2 October 2026. Al Jazeera, citin
establishes: Three outlets report that the order existed. They word its scope slightly differently ("more than five" and "five or more"), and the archive holds no copy of the order, so the wording is a report of it. The order is a written instrument with a date, an issuing office and a text, which is what separates it from the force question on INC-0001. Who issued it is recorded separately at INC-DEL-013. The section number is quoted as the reports give it and has not been checked against the current text of the Sanhita by anyone who practises.

title: The sources disagree on which office issued the section 163 order of 2 October 2026. Al Jazeera, citing The Times of India, says Delhi Police imposed it. Outloo
establishes: Not resolved here. The two answers lead to different custodians and different RTI routes: Delhi Police sits under the Union Home Ministry, while the Delhi government is a separate public authority. Neither source quotes the order or names a signatory. See OQ-055. A further Outlook report, citing Hindustan Times, says Delhi Police imposed the restrictions on the Friday morning, which sits with the Al Jazeera account and against Outlook's own earlier statement that the Delhi government issued the order. The dispute stays open until the order is read.

title: Outlook reports that protesters alleged they were dragged along the road and beaten with batons during the detentions of 2 October 2026, and that a history stud
establishes: These are allegations made by protesters, reported by one outlet, beside a wire report that describes shoving and no more. The archive does not hold footage, a medical record or a police account. None of the articles read for this entry mentions tear gas, pellets or firearms; that is an absence in those articles and not a finding that none were used. See OQ-060.

title: Outlook, Deccan Chronicle and India TV (as carried by tob.news) report that internet services were suspended in the Jantar Mantar area on 2 October 2026. Outloo
establishes: Three outlets report the suspension; none quotes an order. One headline in the 3 October sweep reports the cut ran until 9 pm, but the page was not retrieved and the figure is not recorded here. The July order recorded at INC-DEL-007 shows the form such an order takes and which office signs it, and a suspension order is the kind of instrument the Supreme Court has said must be published (see PREC-SHUT-001). Whether a separate order was made on 2 October, and by whom, is OQ-056. India TV is the origin of the tob.news report and is not independent of it.

title: The Week reports that an independent journalist accused an Assistant Commissioner of Police of hitting her on the chest while she filmed the detention of a stud
establishes: One source for all of it. The officer is named in the source and not here, on the rule the archive applies to a private person and to an unproven allegation: holding a post is not evidence of having done what is alleged. The complaints are allegations and are recorded as such. The Week's text says "sexual assault" while its address says "sexual harassment", so the nature of the complaints is not settled by the source. No complainant is named in the source or here. See OQ-057. Later reporting is recorded at INC-DEL-022: PTI and Deccan Chronicle report that the complaints were of sexual harassment, that no FIR was registered when the journalists went to a police station, and that the New Delhi district transferred the complaints to the Crime Branch for a fair and impartial enquiry. The Week describes the first allegation as a blow to the chest; PTI quotes the complaint as alleging sexual assault. The two wordings are different allegations and neither is resolved here. The three FIRs are recorded at INC-DEL-017.

title: Mumbai Police registered a First Information Report at Shivaji Park police station on 3 October 2026 over the Cockroach Janta Party gathering held at Shivaji Pa
establishes: The same class of record as INC-MAH-002: a case registered for assembling without permission, with no use of force established and none alleged in these sources. A refusal of permission is a written instrument with a date and a signatory, and the FIR is a second one; both can be asked for (OQ-059, FQ-022). The Free Press Journal also reports an altercation between supporters and a group opposing the demonstration after the gathering ended, with police intervening; that is one source and is not a finding about the police. The Supreme Court order of 1 September 2026 recorded at PROC-SC-014 is reported to cover FIRs over the protests of 20 to 25 July; this is a different gathering, and the archive draws no conclusion about how the order bears on it. The sections are quoted as the reports give them and have not been checked against the current text by anyone who practises. Who is named and who complained is DISPUTED at INC-MAH-004.

title: The three sources read for the Mumbai FIR of 3 October 2026 disagree on who it names and who made the complaint. PTI, as carried by The Tribune, identifies one
establishes: Not resolved here, and not resolvable from reporting: the FIR is the document that settles it. The three accounts agree that Abhijeet Dipke is named. Whether the case rests on a private complaint or was registered by the police is a real difference, because it changes which office to ask. The complainant is a private person and is not named in this record. See OQ-058.

title: Three FIRs were registered on 3 October 2026 over the protest of 2 October at Jantar Mantar, at Parliament Street and Connaught Place police stations. Outlook,
establishes: Two reports with different origins (Hindustan Times and PTI) agree on the number, the offences of disobedience and no named accused, and differ in how many sections they list. The FIRs themselves would settle it. Outlook says organisers and participating organisations are mentioned in the FIRs even though none is named as accused. The sections are quoted as the reports give them and have not been checked against the current text by anyone who practises. This supersedes the single-source mention of three FIRs at INC-DEL-016.

title: ThePrint, citing PTI and Delhi Police officials, reports that nearly 200 protesters were detained on Saturday 3 October 2026 as AISA and others returned to Jant
establishes: One outlet for the figure and for the allegation. ThePrint carried an earlier version of the same story with a figure of around 150, so the count moved during the day. The bus allegation is made by a political organisation and is not corroborated here. Section 163 BNSS is described as in force on the Friday; the sources read do not say whether it was extended to Saturday.

title: The News Mill reports, on police sources, that around 15 Delhi Police personnel were injured, some women personnel reportedly by bites, and around 110 people we
establishes: The police account of injuries to police is recorded because it is part of what happened and because an account that holds only protesters' allegations would be one-sided. One outlet, anonymous police sources, no statement on the record. The date is not settled by this source: the page was read as dating the protest to Sunday 5 October, and 5 October 2026 is a Monday; the Sunday of that weekend is 4 October. The archive has not corrected the source and records the date as the Sunday after 3 October.

title: Delhi Police refused permission for the protest planned at Jantar Mantar on 2 October 2026. DT Next reports it on unnamed police sources and says the protest wa
establishes: The Indian Youth Congress order of 1 October is a written instrument with a date, and the Youth Congress has put it before the Delhi High Court (PROC-DEL-005), so a copy exists outside the police. It is the Delhi counterpart of the Maharashtra refusal at INC-MAH-003 and the Kochi notice at INC-KER-001. None of the sources names the officer or office that signed it. See OQ-061 and FQ-023.

title: IBTimes India reports that Delhi Police personnel at the Jantar Mantar protests did not wear name tags, that junior personnel were allowed to remove them while
establishes: One outlet. Hindustan Times and The Times of India headlines in the 5 October sweep carry the same story and were not retrieved. The record matters to this archive for a plain reason: an officer who cannot be identified cannot be asked who gave an order, and the explanation offered concerns harassment of officers and their families, which is a real harm and is recorded as the police's stated reason and not as the archive's view.

title: PTI and Deccan Chronicle report that three women journalists alleged sexual harassment by police personnel during the Jantar Mantar protest of 3 October 2026, t
establishes: The complainants are not named here. PTI reports that an Assistant Commissioner of Police is named in the complaint and could not be reached for comment; the officer is not named in this record, on the rule that an unproven allegation does not put a name in the archive. Deccan Chronicle reports that protesters and opposition figures say police cited the Crime Branch inquiry as the reason for deferring an FIR. Whether an FIR has since been registered is OQ-057. This is the same set of complaints The Week reports at INC-DEL-016, in different words.

title: Bar and Bench reports that the president of the Indian Youth Congress moved the Delhi High Court on 3 October 2026 against Delhi Police's order of 1 October 202
establishes: Two outlets with different origins report the petition and the order of 1 October. The case number is not reported in either. No order on the merits exists yet. The hearing of 12 October is a date to check. Retrieving the petition and the order of 1 October is FQ-023.

title: LiveLaw reports that on 5 October 2026 a bench headed by the Chief Justice of India, Surya Kant, agreed to list a plea seeking directions to Delhi Police to per
establishes: One source retrieved. Other outlets carry the story and were not read. Listing is not a hearing and no order on the merits is recorded. The petition and any order are to be retrieved from the Court's own site, as for FQ-016 and FQ-018.

title: The Tribune reports that on Tuesday 6 October 2026 about 300 opposition MPs marched from Parliament towards the Election Commission headquarters, that police st
establishes: One outlet, and the account of the first day is a summary inside a report about the second. The Wire carries a report headlined as Delhi Police detaining Rahul and Priyanka Gandhi during the INDIA bloc protest, but only its headline could be read, so it is not cited for anything here. The Election Commission is reported elsewhere to have said no party had sought an appointment before the march; that is not recorded here because the page carrying it was not read.

title: On Wednesday 7 October 2026 Delhi Police detained opposition leaders near Jantar Mantar, among them Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra. The Tribune and Sias
establishes: Two outlets agree on who was detained, where they were taken and that they were released the same day. Neither quotes a police statement. Siasat's wording is 'BNS 163', which is the section of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita and not of the Nyaya Sanhita; the archive records it as section 163 and has not corrected the source. Whether an order was in force on 7 October, and whether it is the order of 2 October recorded at INC-DEL-012, is part of OQ-055.

title: The Tribune reports that Priyanka Gandhi Vadra said police assaulted protesters and that she had been scratched and thrown to the ground, that Mahua Moitra alle
establishes: These are allegations by named politicians, reported as theirs. The Tribune also reports that women police personnel removed Priyanka Gandhi Vadra from the road where she was lying down, which is the police side of the same event and is not an allegation. No footage, medical record or police account is held.

title: Siasat, with PTI inputs, refers to an FIR registered against Rahul Gandhi, which Akhilesh Yadav is reported to have tied to the protest of Tuesday 6 October 202
establishes: The FIR is mentioned in a photo caption and in a politician's remark, and the article does not describe it. A search result summarised it as an FIR for entering Akashvani Bhawan without permission; the page read does not say that, and the archive does not record it. See OQ-062.

title: FIR No. 110/2016 was registered at Police Station Vasant Kunj North, Delhi, over the event held at Jawaharlal Nehru University on 9 February 2016. The Delhi Hig
establishes: Both orders name the FIR number and station. The registration date is not stated in either order; the High Court order says in paragraph 27 that the FIR 'has been registered only about three weeks back'. LiveLaw (14 January 2019) gives 11 February 2016 as the registration date, a single secondary source (see HIST-JNU16-002). Sedition is the label the FIR carries; no finding on the merits is recorded here, and the High Court order itself says its observations are not an expression on merits.

title: The FIR was registered on 11 February 2016 against unidentified persons following complaints from a Member of Parliament of the BJP (named in the report as Mahe
establishes: Single secondary source, published 14 January 2019, describing the chargesheet. The complainant detail is not in the two court orders read for this file. A different account is recorded by the State in the High Court (HIST-JNU16-003): that the FIR followed a Zee News telecast of 10 February and raw footage obtained from the channel. Both accounts may be true. The archive has not seen the FIR itself. Obtain the FIR text (Delhi Police publishes FIRs online in many cases; check) to settle complainant and date.

title: In the Delhi High Court on 2 March 2016 the Additional Solicitor General for the State submitted that: permission for a cultural evening at Sabarmati Dhaba, JNU
establishes: VERIFIED only as to what the order records the State as having submitted. The order does not find these facts. It also records the petitioner's contrary account (that he raised no anti-national slogans, that the campus stayed peaceful, and that the video was reported to be doctored) in paragraphs 7 to 9, and the Standing Counsel for the Government of NCT of Delhi saying the petitioner could be released on bail (paragraph 25). This is the only primary document read that describes who informed the police before 12 February; it describes a call to police on 9 February, not an order to enter the campus on 12 February.

title: Kanhaiya Kumar, president of the JNU Students' Union, was arrested by Delhi Police on 12 February 2016 in connection with the sedition case, and was in police c
establishes: The Quint (16 February 2016) and The News Minute (25 February 2016) are independent outlets. The Delhi High Court order of 2 March 2016 (paragraph 8) records the petitioner's submission that he had been remanded to police custody three times; it does not give the arrest date. Whether the arrest took place on campus, and in what manner, is covered at HIST-JNU16-005.

title: Delhi Police went onto the JNU campus on 12 February 2016 and took Kanhaiya Kumar into custody there.
establishes: The claim is widely repeated, but no source fetched for this file states the place, time and manner of the arrest in terms. The Quint (20 February 2016) says the Vice-Chancellor was criticised for not following protocol before police were allowed onto the campus, and gives no date. Onmanorama (15 February 2016) reports a JNU status report saying a letter was sent to police asking them to take utmost precautions before entering the campus, and that police told the university they would enter only if absolutely necessary. Search-result snippets, not read as pages, describe a plainclothes arrest from the campus and raids on hostels on 12 and 13 February; they are not relied on. Not found: a police arrest memo, the case diary entry, or a court record of the place of arrest.

title: A letter dated 11 February 2016 from the JNU Registrar to the Deputy Commissioner of Police, South District, is reported to have said that the Vice-Chancellor g
establishes: Single secondary source read (The Quint, 20 February 2016, which calls it a 'virtual carte blanche'). The letter itself has not been seen; HuffPost India, citing NDTV, is reported in search snippets to describe it as 'purportedly' written by the Registrar, but that page could not be fetched (404 on the redirect) and is not cited as read. The Vice-Chancellor is reported in snippets to have said at a press conference that he did not invite the police; no fetched page carries that statement, so no DISPUTED record can be made yet. Obtain the letter by RTI to JNU and to the Office of the Commissioner of Police, Delhi, and the register entry for it. The Quint also reports a senior professor's claim that the Vice-Chancellor first refused and relented after the Security Officer and the Registrar stressed the gravity of the charges; that is one person's account and is not established.

title: On 22 February 2016 Delhi Police were reported to be waiting outside the JNU campus for the Vice-Chancellor's permission before entering to arrest students who
establishes: The Quint live blog and IANS (via ummid.com) are two reports of one situation on 22 February 2016, which is after the 12 February events. It shows police treating the university's consent as a step they sought, which is relevant context for the question of who authorised entry on 12 February, but it is a different day and not evidence about that day. The IANS report quotes the Delhi Police Commissioner, asked whether police would enter JNU, as saying he was confident his team was competent to deal with the matter and that the investigating officer would choose the best available option.

title: Who gave the order for Delhi Police to enter the JNU campus on 12 February 2016, and who gave the order to arrest Kanhaiya Kumar, is not established by any docu
establishes: No order, requisition, case-diary entry, deployment record or affidavit naming the authorising office has been found. What the documents read do show: (a) the State's account in the High Court of events up to 10 February (HIST-JNU16-003); (b) a reported Registrar's letter of 11 February about university permission (HIST-JNU16-006), which would show the university's consent and does not show who in the police or the Ministry decided to go in; (c) in Parliament, members of the Lok Sabha on 24 February 2016 criticised the Home Minister's public statements and the Commissioner's, and the Minister of Human Resource Development spoke about the permission slip and the university's own enquiry, but the record read contains no statement by the Government on who authorised the entry or the arrest (HIST-JNU16-021). Delhi Police reports to the Ministry of Home Affairs; that structure is stated in this repository's own notes, not established from a source fetched for this file. Routes: RTI to the Ministry of Home Affairs and to the Office of the Commissioner of Police, Delhi, for the arrest memo, the case diary, any requisition to or from JNU, and communications between the two; a question in Parliament; the Delhi High Court record of W.P.(Crl.) 558/2016, including the State's status report.

title: The Delhi High Court (Pratibha Rani J.) granted Kanhaiya Kumar interim bail for six months on 2 March 2016 on a personal bond of Rs 10,000 and one surety, prefe
establishes: The order records at paragraph 27 that 'the investigation has now been transferred to Special Cell'; it does not say which office ordered the transfer or when. The order also records the Government of NCT of Delhi's Standing Counsel supporting bail and the ASG for the State opposing it (paragraphs 18 to 25). Paragraph 56 states the observations are for deciding bail only and are not an expression on merits.

title: On 15 February 2016, at Patiala House Courts Complex, New Delhi, people described in reports as lawyers or persons in lawyers' robes assaulted students, teacher
establishes: Three outlets (The News Minute 25 February 2016; Legally India/IANS 23 July 2016; The News Minute/PTI 24 February 2016). The News Minute and Legally India draw on different wires. The Supreme Court order of 17 February 2016 itself records that 'certain unpleasant and unacceptable incidents are said to have taken place in the court premises' on 15 February (HIST-JNU16-011). Police later charged three lawyers and a Delhi BJP legislator (HIST-JNU16-016). Injury counts are not established (HIST-JNU16-012).

title: The Supreme Court's order of 17 February 2016 in N.D. Jayaprakash v. Union of India, W.P.(Crl.) 25/2016 (Chelameswar and Sapre JJ.), records that on 15 February
establishes: On 22 February 2016 the Court corrected the order on the Solicitor General's submission that on 15 February Kanhaiya Kumar 'was not in fact produced before the Patiala House Court Complex but he was only scheduled to be produced there' (see HIST-JNU16-013). The order was issued the morning of 17 February; the order states the Delhi High Court's administrative side was meeting the same day at 2 pm.

title: The number of people injured at Patiala House Courts on 15 February 2016, and their identities and injuries, is not established by any document read for this fi
establishes: No source fetched gives a count. Not found: Delhi Police FIR texts (reports say four FIRs were registered over the 15 and 17 February violence), medico-legal certificates (these need the consent of the people concerned), or the aggregate admission figures of any hospital. Routes: RTI to government hospitals for aggregate figures; the FIR copies from Delhi Police; the Delhi Police status report and chargesheets of July 2016 (Metropolitan Magistrate Snigdha Sarvaria, per Legally India).

title: On 22 February 2016 the Supreme Court corrected its order of 17 February after the Solicitor General said that on 15 February 2016 Kanhaiya Kumar was not in fac
establishes: This matters for how the 15 February events are described. The reports read describe the 15 February attack as on students, teachers and journalists, and the attacks on Kanhaiya Kumar himself as on 17 February 2016 (The News Minute, PTI 24 February 2016). Some other outlets, in snippets not read as pages, put an attack on him on 15 February; the court's correction is the better record. The 22 February order also lists the reports then before the Court (HIST-JNU16-015).

title: The Supreme Court on 17 February 2016 recorded that it deputed six members of the Bar (Kapil Sibal, Rajeev Dhawan, Dushyant Dave, H.P. Rawal, Ajit K. Sinha and
establishes: The Committee is a group of advocates deputed by the Court. The group is described in some reports as a 'commission'; the order does not use that word. One member, Mr Sinha, appeared for the Commissioner of Police, Delhi at the same hearing; the order and later orders show him continuing to appear for Delhi Police (for example on 22 February). Reports differ on the size of the team (one PTI report lists seven names for a six-member team); the order lists six.

title: At about 4 pm on 17 February 2016 the Committee returned and made an oral report; the Supreme Court asked for it in writing. The order records: 'it is reported
establishes: The order records only that the accused was manhandled and does not record what the Committee said about police conduct. The office the Court addressed is the Commissioner of Police, Delhi, named by office. The order does not name the person.

title: The written report of the Supreme Court's Committee of advocates, a pen drive of the video one member recorded on his phone, and other reports were filed in sea
establishes: The text of the Committee's written report has not been obtained and is not in any document read. The 22 February order also says the Delhi High Court's administrative committee proceedings were not supplied. The 23 February order directs the Registry to mask the Registrar General's identity in copies of the visuals and to verify the pen drive against Mr Raval's phone. Where to look: the Supreme Court registry for the sealed-cover records and any later unsealing, and the Delhi High Court Registrar General's report.

title: Members of the Supreme Court's Committee told the Court orally on 17 February 2016 that the police did not do their job at Patiala House Courts. PTI reports Mr
establishes: These are statements by Committee members as reported, and allegations from them. The Supreme Court order of the same day records only that the accused was manhandled (HIST-JNU16-015). The News Minute quotes the written report as saying 'the atmosphere outside was surcharged and intimidating' and that there was 'an effort to create an atmosphere of fear and terror', quoted via LiveLaw, and says the report records that Mr Dhawan and Mr Sibal asked police how a person not on the Supreme Court's list could enter the courtroom without a satisfactory reply. The LiveLaw piece (27 January 2018) is an opinion article by a lawyer. The three sources all depend on the same oral and written report and are not independent of it; they are independent of one another as outlets. The 17 February events concern Kanhaiya Kumar's court appearance, not the 15 February attack.

title: Delhi Police conduct at Patiala House Courts on 15 February 2016, what officers present did or did not do and on whose instructions, is not established by any d
establishes: The Supreme Court Committee's findings, the NHRC team's findings and the Bar Council affidavit concern mainly 17 February. For 15 February the only primary document read is the Supreme Court order recording that 'unpleasant and unacceptable incidents are said to have taken place'. The Lok Sabha record of 24 February 2016 carries members' statements that police 'stood as a mute spectator' (HIST-JNU16-021), which are members' allegations. A complaint to the NHRC, reproduced in its press release, alleges police 'remained mute spectators' (HIST-JNU16-019). Not found: the Delhi Police report to the Supreme Court (due 19 February 2016), deployment orders and duty rosters for 15 February, station diary or control-room entries, or the Registrar General's report. Routes: RTI to the Office of the Commissioner of Police, Delhi and the DCP concerned; the Supreme Court record of the sealed reports; the Delhi High Court Registrar General.

title: The National Human Rights Commission issued a notice on 17 February 2016 to the Union Home Secretary, the Chief Secretary of the Government of NCT of Delhi and
establishes: VERIFIED as to what the Commission's press release says; the allegations are the complainant's, not a finding. The reply reports are not found. LiveLaw (26 February 2016) says the NHRC report said Kumar was subjected to psychological pressure during questioning and cited serious dereliction of duty by Delhi Police for not preventing the assault or apprehending attackers; this is one secondary report of an NHRC team report, which has not been seen, and is not recorded as established. Obtain the NHRC case file and reply from the Delhi Police Commissioner.

title: An NHRC fact-finding team report is reported to have found the assault on Kanhaiya Kumar in the court premises 'organized and pre-planned' and to have recorded
establishes: Reported by LiveLaw on 26 February 2016 as part of a petition's attachments. Other outlets (India TV, Hindustan Times via PressReader) could not be read (403). The NHRC report itself has not been seen. Locate it through the NHRC case record or the petition annexures in the Supreme Court.

title: The Lok Sabha debated 'the situation arising out of recent incidents in institutions of higher education' on 24 February 2016. The record shows members stating
establishes: VERIFIED as to the content of the debate record, which is a primary document. The statements are members' statements, not findings. The record is long (several hundred thousand characters) and was searched for the Home Minister, police, Commissioner, Patiala House, permission and Vice-Chancellor, not read in full. A written reply by the Ministry of Home Affairs to a Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha question on these events was not found; searching sansad.in for starred and unstarred questions of the February to March 2016 sessions is the route.

title: Delhi Police registered four FIRs over the violence at Patiala House Courts on 15 and 17 February 2016, arrested three lawyers (Vikram Singh Chauhan, Yashpal Si
establishes: Legally India/IANS (15 May 2016) and The News Minute/PTI (24 February 2016) are different wires. The News Minute reported that as of 24 February Yashpal Singh had been arrested after surrendering at Tilak Marg police station, Om Sharma had been arrested on a Saturday and bailed, and Vikram Singh Chauhan had not responded to notices; the Delhi Police Commissioner is quoted saying police had summoned the lawyers repeatedly and had 'the option of taking coercive action'. The persons named are those the police arrested or charged; no finding of guilt is recorded here. Police took about three months to identify the assailants from CCTV, per Legally India.

title: Delhi Police filed three chargesheets on 19 July 2016 before Metropolitan Magistrate Snigdha Sarvaria: against three lawyers for the 15 February attack on journ
establishes: Single secondary source (Legally India, from IANS, 23 July 2016); statute numbers are not given. The chargesheets themselves have not been seen. Later outcomes (search snippets, not read as pages, mention an acquittal in October 2021 in a separate case) are not recorded. Obtain the chargesheets and orders from the Patiala House court record.

title: The Supreme Court on 26 February 2016 issued notice on a petition by advocate Kamini Jaiswal seeking a Special Investigation Team probe into the Patiala House v
establishes: Single secondary source. Attribution: the statements from the sting are the speakers' claims as reported by LiveLaw ('officers were in uniform, that's why they (too) were not thrashing him'); they are not findings and the footage has not been seen. See HIST-JNU16-025 for a conflicting report of this hearing and HIST-JNU16-026 for the outcome.

title: India Legal reported on 26 February 2016 that the Supreme Court 'directed the Delhi Police to set up an SIT' to investigate the 15 and 17 February violence; Liv
establishes: Version 1 (India Legal): the headline and first sentence say the Court directed an SIT, while its body says the petition was 'demanding' one and asks why a fresh petition was filed. Version 2 (LiveLaw): notice only.
